frames.narration: PrintShop wants to read photos. It makes a random code_verifier, hashes it into a code_challenge (S256), picks a random state, and opens the browser at /authorize with scope=openid photos.read.
The auth server checks redirect_uri against the registered value (exact match), then the user signs in and sees what PrintShop asks for. The password goes to the auth server only.
The user approves. The server stores the code with the challenge and redirects to printshop://cb?code=...&state=.... The code is valid for 60 seconds and works once.
On a phone, any app registered for the printshop:// scheme can receive that URL. The malicious app now holds the code and the state, but not the verifier.
The attacker races to the token endpoint. The server finds no code_verifier to hash against the stored challenge and refuses with invalid_grant. Without PKCE this request would have succeeded.
PrintShop calls POST /token on the back channel with the code and its code_verifier. The server computes BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)) and finds it equal to the stored challenge.

The server returns an access token (3600 s), a refresh token, and, because of the openid scope, an ID token that says who signed in (sub, aud=printshop, nonce). PrintShop validates the ID token; the access token is not proof of login.
PrintShop calls the Photo API with the bearer access token. The API checks signature, expiry, audience and that photos.read covers GET /photos, and returns the photos. The password was never shared.
